source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial
finding: Founding RCT. Physicians with GPT-4 plus usual tools did not reason better than physicians with usual tools alone.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), single-blind, 6 vignettes. Median score 76% (IQR 66-87) with GPT-4 vs 74% (63-84) conventional. Adjusted diff 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60).
limits: One model, no prompt training, 6 curated vignettes, rubric score not patient outcome. Power was >80% only for an 8-point gap.
agent_relevance: Giving a strong model to a human does not by itself lift the human. Our agent should not count on a person adding value to its answer.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (LLM alone arm)
finding: GPT-4 run alone (3 runs) beat the physicians who had GPT-4 in hand.
numbers: LLM alone median 92% (IQR 82-97), 16 points above the conventional group (95% CI 2-30, P=.03). Physician+GPT-4 76%.
limits: Exploratory arm; prompts were written by the study team, not by the physicians. Cases were never public.
agent_relevance: A gap of about 16 points between model alone and human+model shows the loss is in the human-model interface, not in the model.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (subgroups, time, accuracy)
finding: No subgroup gained: not attendings, not residents, not frequent LLM users. Time and final-diagnosis accuracy moved only a little.
numbers: Attendings diff 0.5 (P=.92); residents 3 (P=.50); LLM use more than monthly 5 (-7 to 16); less than monthly -0.5. Time 519s vs 565s (diff -82s, 95% CI -195 to 31). Final diagnosis OR 1.4 (0.7-2.8) ordinal; 1.9 (0.9-4.0) binary.
limits: Small subgroups; wide CIs. Table and text disagree on some numbers (time P .20 vs .15; 22 vs 25 users).
agent_relevance: No evidence that practice or seniority fixes the interface problem. Design the scaffold, not the user.

source: Goh et al. (2025) GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial (Nature Medicine)
finding: Follow-up RCT on management reasoning. This time GPT-4 help gave a small, significant gain.
numbers: 92 physicians (67 attendings, 25 residents), 5 vignettes. Total score 43.0% (SD 17.3) with GPT-4 vs 35.7% (SD 15.5) control. Diff 6.5 points (95% CI 2.7-10.2, P<.001). Diagnostic sub-score +12.1 (3.1-21.0). Time per case 801s vs 690s (+119s, P=.022).
limits: Text and abstract disagree on the sign of the LLM-alone vs LLM-assisted difference. Incorrect answers not penalised. Harm rated by one reviewer. No Cohen d reported (rough d about 0.4, our estimate).
agent_relevance: Assist works better on open management tasks where the rubric credits extra content, and costs time. Adjusting for response length cut the gain to 3.7 points, so coverage credit may reward longer answers.

source: Goh et al. (2025) management reasoning RCT: LLM alone and harm
finding: In the management trial the model alone matched the assisted physicians, and its gain over controls was not significant.
numbers: LLM alone 43.7% vs control 35.7%: diff 7.3 (95% CI -0.7 to 15.4, P=.074). LLM alone vs LLM-assisted about 0.9 points (P=.8). Severe-harm rating 7.6% vs 7.5%.
limits: Only 25 LLM-alone scored cases. Harm outcome exploratory.
agent_relevance: Two RCTs by the same group differ: diagnosis task no gain, management task small gain. Effect depends on task and rubric, so do not generalise from one trial.

source: Kanjee, Crowe, Rodman (2023) Accuracy of a Generative AI Model in a Complex Diagnostic Challenge (JAMA)
finding: GPT-4 on 70 NEJM clinicopathologic conference cases from 2021-2022 put the final diagnosis in its differential about 2 times in 3.
numbers: Final diagnosis in differential 64% (45/70). Top diagnosis correct 39% (27/70). Mean rank of right answer 2.5 (SD 2.5). Mean list length 9.0. Quality score mean 4.2 (SD 1.3). Rater agreement 66%, kappa 0.57.
limits: Cases dated after most training data (cutoff Sept 2021) but contamination not tested. Some case information left out of the prompt. Teaching cases, not routine care.
agent_relevance: The baseline every later paper compares to. Shows how fast numbers moved (64% to 78% to 85%+ in about three years).

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (NEJM CPC)
finding: o1-preview raised the 2023 GPT-4 result on the same published cases.
numbers: 143 NEJM CPCs: correct dx in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8); first dx correct 52%. On the 70 shared cases: o1 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9% (P=.015). Correct next test chosen 87.5%. Before vs after training cutoff 79.8% vs 73.5% (P=.59).
limits: Cutoff test has low power; cases may be in training data. Rater kappa on test plan only 0.28 (class imbalance). Model-only, no human use.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-style models improve differential generation by about 16 points on the same set. Supports extended deliberation at the point of diagnosis.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (NEJM Healer R-IDEA)
finding: o1-preview wrote documented clinical reasoning that scored perfect far more often than humans or GPT-4.
numbers: Perfect R-IDEA score 78/80 for o1-preview vs 47/80 GPT-4, 28/80 attendings, 16/80 residents (all P<.0001). Cannot-miss diagnoses included: median 0.92, not significantly different from humans.
limits: Humans and GPT-4 are historical controls from earlier studies. Score rewards written reasoning, not correctness.
agent_relevance: The model beats people on the form of reasoning but not on listing dangerous diagnoses. A cannot-miss check is not made redundant.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (management and landmark cases)
finding: On management vignettes o1 far outscored physicians; on diagnostic landmark cases it was near ceiling with no clear gap.
numbers: Management (5 cases): o1 median 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians+GPT-4 41%, physicians conventional 34%; o1 +49.0 points vs conventional (95% CI 31.7-66.3). Landmark (6 cases): o1 97% vs GPT-4 92%, phys+GPT-4 76%, conventional 74%; diff vs conventional 20.2 (95% CI -0.4 to 40.9, P=.055).
limits: Only 5 and 6 cases. Human data are historical. Ceiling effect on landmark cases.
agent_relevance: Same cases as Goh 2024: human with GPT-4 stays at 76%, newer model alone reaches 97%. Model progress, not human use, drives the gain.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (real ER second opinions)
finding: On 79 real emergency cases o1 gave better differentials than two attendings at each of three time points, blinded.
numbers: Exact or very close dx: o1 65.8%, 69.6%, 79.7% at triage, ER physician, admission. Physician 1: 54.4, 60.8, 75.9. Physician 2: 48.1, 50.6, 68.4. Raters could not tell source: 83.5% and 84.6% 'can't tell'.
limits: Only two comparison physicians; text notes only; not a prospective trial; scored on diagnosis, while ER work is triage and disposition.
agent_relevance: Gap is widest when information is least (triage). This is the use case for a differential generator on thin data.

source: Bean et al. (2025) Clinical knowledge in LLMs does not translate to human interactions (Oxford RCT)
finding: Large randomized trial with the public: LLMs that score high alone did not help lay users.
numbers: 1,298 UK adults, 10 scenarios, 3 LLMs (GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+) vs control. Models alone: conditions identified 94.9%, disposition 56.3%. With users: conditions below 34.5%, disposition below 44.2%, no better than control (43.0%). Control had 1.76x odds (95% CI 1.45-2.13) of naming a relevant condition.
limits: Lay users, not clinicians. Scenarios written by 3 doctors. Models from 2024.
agent_relevance: Strongest failure of 'good model = good system'. Information was lost on the way in and out.

source: Bean et al. (2025): where the loss happens
finding: Two breakdowns: users give partial information, then do not use correct suggestions.
numbers: In chats GPT-4o raised a relevant condition 65.7 (+/-6.2)% of the time, Llama 3 67.0%, Command R+ 73.2%. LLMs suggested 2.21 conditions per chat, only 34.0% correct (95% CI 32.3-35.9). Users listed 1.33 conditions, 38.7% correct.
limits: Gold labels from 3 doctors; conversation analysis partly coded by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Our agent should ask for missing data itself instead of waiting for the user to supply it, and should state its final answer clearly.

source: Bean et al. (2025): benchmarks and simulated users do not predict human outcome
finding: MedQA scores and LLM-simulated patients failed to predict real user results.
numbers: Models beat users on MedQA in 20/20 (GPT-4o), 19/20 (Llama 3), 17/20 (Command R+) scenarios; benchmark scores above 80% matched human scores below 20% in several. Simulated users: 57.3% disposition, 60.7% conditions. Regression of simulated on real, conditions: -0.01 +/- 0.34 (GPT-4o).
limits: Simulation used the same LLM family on both sides.
agent_relevance: Do not trust LLM-simulated users or exam scores as a proxy for deployment. Test with real humans.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making (Nature Medicine)
finding: On 2,400 real MIMIC-IV abdominal-pain cases, open Llama-2-family models diagnosed worse than hospitalists and worse still when they had to gather the data.
numbers: 80-patient reader study vs 4 hospitalists: models 16-25 points behind (P<.001). Hospitalists 87.5% (German resident) to 92.5% (US). Autonomous run: Llama 2 Chat 45.5% vs 58.8% full-info; OASST 54.9% vs 67.8%; WizardLM 53.9% vs 65.1%.
limits: Only Llama-2 models (GPT-4 not allowed on MIMIC data). Four clinicians. Four diagnoses only. Old models; later models likely better.
agent_relevance: Models are weaker as a self-directed workup than as a second reader. A scaffold should give structure for information gathering.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making (Nature Medicine) (guideline adherence, labs)
finding: Models skipped needed exams and could not read lab values against a reference range.
numbers: Physical exam requested: Llama 2 Chat 98.1%, OASST 87.7%, WizardLM 63.9%. Lab-value classification for low results: 26.5%, 70.2%, 45.8%; for high results 50.1%, 77.2%, 24.1%. Instruction errors every 2-4 patients; invented tools every 2-5 patients.
limits: Open models of 2023. Simple numeric checks are now often done by code tools.
agent_relevance: Do lab comparison and counting in code, not in the model (program decides, model fills slots).

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making (Nature Medicine) (robustness: wording and information amount)
finding: Small wording changes and more information both changed accuracy, and more information often hurt.
numbers: Swapping 'final diagnosis' for 'main diagnosis': up to +7.0 / down to -10.6 points. Cholecystitis +18.5 (Chat) and +16.5 (WizardLM) when only radiology reports shown; pancreatitis +21.6 (Chat) with labs only.
limits: Effects are per-pathology and per-model; direction varies.
agent_relevance: More context is not safer: give the data relevant to the current question, in stages.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine (npj Digital Medicine)
finding: Clinical-style reasoning prompts (differential, Bayesian, analytic, intuitive) did not beat plain chain-of-thought for GPT-4. For GPT-3.5 most were worse.
numbers: Modified MedQA free-response. GPT-3.5: CoT 46%; intuitive 48% (P=.9); analytic 40% (P=.001); differential 38% (P<.001); Bayesian 42% (P=.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%; intuitive 77%, differential 78% (P=.24), analytic 78% (P=.35), Bayesian 72% (P=.07).
limits: Exam questions, not patients. Rationale quality not verified here.
agent_relevance: Imposing human reasoning forms is free on strong models, harmful on weak ones. Keep forced-structure operators optional and signal-triggered (G1).

source: Takita et al. (2025) A systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic performance comparison between generative AI and physicians (npj Digital Medicine)
finding: Across 83 studies (to June 2024), generative AI was on par with non-experts and worse than experts.
numbers: Pooled AI accuracy 52.1% (95% CI 47.0-57.1). Physicians overall 9.9 points higher (CI -2.3 to 22.0, P=.10). Non-experts 0.6 higher (-14.5 to 15.7, P=.93). Experts 15.8 higher (4.4-27.1, P=.007).
limits: 63/83 (76%) studies at high risk of bias (PROBAST); small test sets; unknown training data. Mostly GPT-3.5/GPT-4-era models.
agent_relevance: Expert-level claim was not established by the pooled literature before reasoning models. Evidence quality is low.

source: Takita et al. (2025) A systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic performance comparison between generative AI and physicians (npj Digital Medicine) (model-by-model)
finding: Newer models closed the expert gap; older ones did not.
numbers: No significant difference from experts for GPT-4V, GPT-4o, Llama 3 70B, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Perplexity. Significantly worse than experts: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2, Llama 3 8B, PaLM2, Mistral 7B, Mixtral, Med-42.
limits: Per-model subgroups are small; non-significance is not proof of equivalence.
agent_relevance: Model-version effect is large; compare across papers only after matching model generation.

source: McDuff et al. (2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models (Nature)
finding: Randomized reader study of an LLM tuned for differential diagnosis (AMIE) on 302 NEJM cases. The LLM alone and as an aid beat clinicians.
numbers: 20 clinicians, 302 cases, each read by two. Top-10 accuracy: AMIE alone 59.1%; unassisted clinicians 33.6% (P=.04). Assisted by AMIE 51.7% vs clinicians unassisted 36.1% (McNemar P<.01) and with search 44.4% (P=.03). Top-1 about 29%. AMIE added the right dx in 73 cases vs 37 for search.
limits: Clinicians had images and tables, AMIE text only. NEJM CPCs possibly seen in training. Not a live workflow.
agent_relevance: Unlike Goh 2024, assisted clinicians did improve here, perhaps because the LLM was tuned for the DDx task and the task was a list. A tuned differential tool may transfer better than a general chatbot.

source: Tu et al. (2024) Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI (AMIE)
finding: In a blinded text-chat OSCE, a tuned LLM beat primary care physicians on most axes.
numbers: 149 scenarios, 20 PCPs, validated patient actors, 23 specialists rating. AMIE better on 28 of 32 axes (specialists) and 24 of 26 axes (patient actors). Higher DDx accuracy; some auto-evaluated top-k gaps not significant.
limits: Text chat is unfamiliar to clinicians; actors, not real patients; the paper itself warns of limits.
agent_relevance: History-taking can be learned in simulated self-play, but Bean et al. showed simulators may not predict real users.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO)
finding: Interactive benchmark: 304 NEJM cases turned into stepwise encounters with costs. A scaffold of virtual physician roles raised accuracy and cut cost.
numbers: Physicians: 19.9% accuracy at $2,963 per case (56 test cases, 11.8 min). GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO with o3: 81.9% at $4,735; 79.9% at $2,396; 85.5% at $7,184 with ensembling.
limits: Generalist physicians barred from search, colleagues and books; no healthy or benign cases, so no false-positive rate; first-order cost estimates; possible memorisation of NEJM cases.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue to our scaffold approach: an orchestrator over a fixed model beat the bare model on cost and accuracy.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO) (generality)
finding: The scaffold helped across model families, most for weaker models; accuracy gains were small for reasoning models.
numbers: MAI-DxO improved models from OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek and Llama families. Accuracy gains smaller for o-series models (o3 78.6 to 81.9); cost efficiency improved most there. Built on GPT-4.1; held-out 56 cases for test.
limits: Dev and test cases from the same source; gains for o3 modest.
agent_relevance: Scaffold value on accuracy shrinks as the base model improves, but it persists on cost. Plan measurements per model tier.

source: Automation Bias in Large Language Model-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among AI-Trained Physicians (medRxiv 2025; NEJM AI 2026)
finding: Randomized trial: physicians given deliberately wrong ChatGPT-4o advice did worse than those given correct advice, even after AI training.
numbers: 44 physicians in Pakistan (22 vs 22), 6 vignettes, 3 with planted errors. Rubric accuracy 84.9% (SD 19.7) with correct advice vs 73.3% (SD 30.5) with flawed; adjusted diff -14.0 points (95% CI -19.7 to -8.3). Top-choice accuracy 90.5% vs 76.1%.
limits: Abstract only (via Europe PMC); full text not opened. Small N; single country; planted errors.
agent_relevance: Wrong model output is followed. Supports G4: fluent agreement is not proof, and the agent should show its evidence so it can be checked.

source: Bedi et al. (2025) Testing and Evaluation of Health Care Applications of Large Language Models: A Systematic Review (JAMA)
finding: Most LLM health studies are not on real patient data.
numbers: 519 studies (Jan 2022-Feb 2024): only 5% used real patient care data; 44.5% tested medical knowledge such as licensing exams; 19.5% diagnosis; 95.4% used accuracy as main measure; calibration or uncertainty 1.2%; bias 15.8%.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Keyword-based classification.
agent_relevance: Much of the LLM-vs-physician literature is exam-style. Weigh real-data and human-in-loop studies more.

source: Cross-study contrast: Goh 2024 vs Brodeur 2024 on identical six landmark cases
finding: Same six cases, same physician arms: GPT-4 alone 92%, o1 97%, physicians with GPT-4 76%, physicians alone 74%.
numbers: Medians: o1 97% (IQR 95-100); GPT-4 92% (82-97); physician+GPT-4 76% (66-87); physician conventional 74% (63-84). o1 vs conventional +20.2 points (95% CI -0.4 to 40.9).
limits: Cross-trial comparison with historical controls; not randomised.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern: model alone is far above human with model, which is about equal to human alone.

source: Our synthesis of Goh 2024, Goh 2025, McDuff 2025, Bean 2025: moderators of human-LLM team gain
finding: Team gains range from none to modest: +2 points (diagnosis, P=.60), +6.5 (management, P<.001), top-10 accuracy 51.7% vs 36.1% (tuned DDx tool vs unaided clinicians), and worse than control for lay users on conditions.
numbers: Goh 2024: +2 (CI -4 to 8). Goh 2025: +6.5 (2.7-10.2). McDuff: 51.7% vs 36.1% top-10. Bean: control odds 1.76 higher.
limits: Different tasks, raters, rubrics and populations; not a formal meta-analysis; our own reading.
agent_relevance: Moderators that seem to matter: tuned vs general model, list-generation vs free reasoning, clinician vs lay user, and rubric that credits coverage.
